title: Piloting agents in GitHub Copilot - Christopher Harrison, Microsoft

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The workshop focuses on GitHub Copilot as a coding agent for code generation, test running, self-healing, and PR-based review workflows. Copilot is explicitly positioned as an AI pair programmer and coding assistant used within IDE and PR contexts. Coverage spans development via code generation, testing via CI and test execution, and deployment via PR creation through GitHub Actions. The workshop assumes GitHub and software development familiarity but introduces Copilot agent features from the ground up. Structured as a hands-on workshop with lab exercises, live demos, and audience Q&A. Twenty transcript evidence anchors with direct quotes ground every major claim.

summary: Christopher Harrison leads a hands-on workshop on GitHub Copilot's agent capabilities at the AI Engineer World's Fair, positioning Copilot as an AI pair programmer. He stresses that context extends beyond prompts to readable code, meaningful comments, and clear project structure. The workshop covers multiple workloads: code completion, chat (ask/edit modes), local agent mode (project exploration, test running, self-healing), and Copilot Coding Agent (autonomous issue completion). Due to Wi-Fi and access issues, Harrison pivots from hands-on labs to live demos and Q&A. He demonstrates the Copilot Coding Agent with a real issue for creating game endpoints, emphasizing that asynchronous work demands clear, specific context to avoid unwanted results. He details copilot-instructions.md—providing high-level project overviews, coding standards, language guidance, and repository structure—available across chat and coding agent modes. He explains prompt files as task-specific instructions with apply-to file path patterns. For coding agent environment setup, he shows the copilot setup steps GitHub Action for installing dependencies. He views a live PR session demonstrating Copilot's behind-the-scenes project exploration. He addresses org-level instructions through native settings, MCP servers, and newly announced Copilot Spaces. In the final Q&A, Harrison details coding agent's security model: it runs in ephemeral GitHub Actions spaces, has read-only repo access except for a copilot-fix-<issue> branch, and has a locked-down firewall with no external access unless explicitly opened. He stresses that introducing AI does not change DevOps fundamentals—code review, testing, linting, and security scans still apply. He explains that Copilot PRs do not automatically run CI workflows; users must manually trigger them after reviewing code. He confirms remote MCP servers are supported with coding agent but require firewall configuration. Issue assignment is GitHub-only currently; Jira/ADO users could script issue copying as a workaround. For external and internal libraries, he advises showing Copilot usage patterns rather than source code, listing APIs in instruction files, or using MCP servers. He notes Copilot does not currently support fine-tuning due to the challenge of distinguishing good code from legacy code, recommending MCP servers as a control mechanism instead. The workshop closes with an apology for network issues and a pointer to the lab materials.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Workshop logistics and announcements
sections.summary: Harrison announces the room is full, the same lab repeats at 3:30 PM, and attendees need to accept GitHub organization invitations via email to access Copilot.

sections.title: Introduction to GitHub Copilot as AI pair programmer
sections.summary: Harrison introduces Copilot as an AI pair programmer with strengths and weaknesses, previewing modes: agent mode, edit mode, ask mode, and Copilot Coding Agent.

sections.title: Context and helping Copilot help you
sections.summary: Using a brunch anecdote, Harrison illustrates iterative context-building. Context includes readable code, comments, and project structure—not just prompts. He advises providing intent, clarity, and specificity.

sections.title: Copilot workloads overview
sections.summary: Harrison surveys Copilot workloads: code completion, chat ask mode, edit mode, local agent mode (explores projects, runs builds/tests, self-heals), and Copilot Coding Agent (assign issues to Copilot).

sections.title: Lab setup and access instructions
sections.summary: Harrison urges attendees to read all instructions first. He directs them to a lab README URL, explains Codespaces setup, and specifies creating repos under the Octo organization with their GitHub handle as repo name.

sections.title: Access issues and lab scope clarification
sections.summary: Many attendees lack Copilot Pro Plus or Enterprise access needed for the Coding Agent portion. Harrison clarifies the rest works with Copilot Free and pivots to a walkthrough approach.

sections.title: Audience Q&A: vibe coding and competitors
sections.summary: Harrison addresses whether agent-driven modes constitute vibe coding (acknowledging they somewhat do) and declines to compare Copilot against Cursor, Windsurf, or Cascade.

sections.title: Introduction to Model Context Protocol (MCP)
sections.summary: Harrison introduces MCP as a way to extend Copilot beyond its static LLM via MCP servers. He shows an architecture diagram, gives examples, lists first-party servers, warns about trust, and notes DDL in custom instructions as a simpler alternative.

sections.title: Pivot to live demos and Copilot Coding Agent demonstration
sections.summary: Harrison pivots to live demos given Wi-Fi issues. He shows a GitHub issue for creating and editing game endpoints, emphasizing that coding agent's asynchronous nature makes clear context critical—ambiguity risks unwanted results.

sections.title: Custom instructions: copilot-instructions.md
sections.summary: Harrison details copilot-instructions.md, a markdown file with high-level project overviews, coding standards, language guidance, and repository structure. It is automatically considered in chat and coding agent modes. He encourages creating one if it doesn't exist.

sections.title: Copilot setup steps and viewing PR sessions
sections.summary: Harrison explains coding agent uses GitHub Actions with a special 'copilot setup steps' action for installing dependencies. He views a live PR Copilot created three minutes prior, showing the session where Copilot explores the project independently.

sections.title: Instructions in chat modes and prompt files
sections.summary: Harrison demonstrates instructions availability in chat agent mode (using Claude 3.5 Sonnet, no personal model preference). He explains prompt files as task-specific instructions applicable manually or automatically via 'apply to' file path patterns, and notes all instruction files become part of the repository.

sections.title: Org-level instructions, Copilot Spaces, and Q&A
sections.summary: Harrison addresses org-level standards via native org-level instructions, MCP servers for searching, and newly announced Copilot Spaces for knowledge bases on github.com. He clarifies coding agent cannot edit its own workflow file once launched, and shows test execution in the session log with failures due to a SQLAlchemy update.

sections.title: Coding agent security model and DevOps fundamentals
sections.summary: Harrison details coding agent's security: ephemeral GitHub Actions runners, read-only repo access except for a copilot-fix-<issue> branch, and a locked-down firewall preventing external access including package installation. He demonstrates that Copilot PRs do not auto-run CI workflows—users must manually trigger them after reviewing code. He emphasizes that DevOps fundamentals (code review, testing, linting, security scans) remain unchanged when using AI.

sections.title: MCP configuration, issue sources, external libraries, and fine-tuning
sections.summary: Harrison confirms remote MCP servers work with coding agent but require firewall configuration in settings. Issue assignment is GitHub-only; Jira/ADO users could script issue copying. For external libraries, he advises showing Copilot usage examples, listing APIs in instructions, or using MCP servers rather than exposing source code. He notes fine-tuning is unsupported due to difficulty distinguishing good from bad code, recommending MCP servers as a control mechanism. The workshop closes with an apology for network issues and a pointer to lab materials.
